one_liner: Header-only C++14/Eigen proximal interior-point convex QP solver; fastest and most robust on Maros-Meszaros, well ahead of OSQP.
what_it_does: Solves convex quadratic programs min 1/2 x'Px + c'x subject to Ax = b, h_l <= Gx <= h_u and x_l <= x <= x_u. The C++ API has piqp::DenseSolver<T> and piqp::SparseSolver<T, I>, each with setup(P, c, A, b, G, h_l, h_u, x_l, x_u), solve() and an allocation-free update(...) for re-solves; there are also C, Python, Matlab/Octave and R interfaces. It is not a drop-in for OSQP: the C interface is only modelled on OSQP's, and problem data are passed as Eigen dense or CSC matrices.
how_it_is_fast: It combines an infeasible primal-dual interior-point method with the proximal method of multipliers (an adaptation of Pougkakiotis and Gondzio), so it converges in a few dozen Newton steps to tight tolerances and tolerates rank-deficient constraints and ill-conditioning, where the ADMM in OSQP needs many cheap iterations and stalls at high accuracy. Each step solves a regularized KKT system with a modified SuiteSparse LDL (sparse, AMD ordering), a dense Cholesky, or a Blasfeo-based multistage backend for MPC-structured problems, with Ruiz equilibration and iterative refinement. Most of the speed ratio comes from far fewer failed or stalled solves rather than from cheaper iterations.
when_to_use: Small-to-medium convex QPs that must be solved to 1e-6 to 1e-9 accuracy, where OSQP often stalls (qpbenchmark high accuracy: PIQP solved 73% of Maros-Meszaros vs OSQP 26%)
Hard or ill-conditioned problems with degenerate or dependent constraints: PIQP solved 94-97% of the 138 problems at low, mid and default accuracy
Model predictive control and other repeated solves with fixed sparsity: update() re-solves without allocating, and the sparse_multistage backend exploits stage structure
Embedding in C++ code that already uses Eigen (header-only, BSD-2 core), or in Python, Matlab, Octave or R through prebuilt packages
when_not_to_use: Very large sparse QPs where one KKT factorization is too costly in memory or time; first-order methods such as OSQP or SCS only need matrix-vector products and a cheaper factorization
Fast warm-started low-accuracy MPC loops are OSQP's home ground; this catalog has no matched warm-start comparison
Nonconvex QPs, mixed-integer or conic (SOCP/SDP) problems are out of scope; use Clarabel, MOSEK or Gurobi
Code paths that enable preconditioner_scale_cost with bounds near zero: open issue #37 (v0.6.1-0.6.2) reports false PRIMAL_INFEASIBLE results on feasible problems
Strict BSD-only licensing needs: the sparse backend is derived from SuiteSparse LDL, whose LGPL-2.1+ notice ships next to it

integration.dependencies: Eigen >= 3.3 (Eigen 5 supported since 0.6.3); optional Blasfeo for the sparse_multistage backend; optional OpenMP; pybind11 and cpu_features for the Python bindings
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (C++17 if built with std::optional or std::filesystem), CMake 3.21+ for the CMake build
integration.platforms: any platform Eigen supports; PyPI wheels for Linux x86-64/aarch64/i686 (glibc and musl), macOS x86-64/arm64 and Windows x64
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each solver is a self-contained object, and OpenMP parallelism is opt-in (BUILD_WITH_OPENMP=OFF by default)

gotchas: Default tolerances are tight (eps_abs 1e-8, eps_rel 1e-9, duality-gap check on) against OSQP's 1e-3, so comparisons at default settings compare different accuracy targets

Versions before 0.6.4 (released 2026-08-28) have an out-of-bounds read in inequality dual recovery (#42) that caused intermittent PIQP_MAX_ITER_REACHED on identical inputs; 0.6.0 also brought a segfault report (#31) and new PRIMAL_INFEASIBLE results (#33), both closed, so pin 0.6.4 or later
The default KKT solver is dense_cholesky; sparse problems need SparseSolver or one of the sparse_ldlt* backends
BUILD_WITH_EIGEN_MAX_ALIGN_BYTES and template-instantiation options affect Eigen ABI compatibility when you link the prebuilt library into code built with different Eigen alignment
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Against ProxQP (ProxSuite) and QPALM, the other OSQP-beaters here, PIQP leads both runtime and success rate on Maros-Meszaros in the independent qpbenchmark (ProxQP 5.9-53x and QPALM 2.2-4.8x slower by shifted geometric mean). Choose ProxQP for dense, robotics-style QPs, where its own benchmark is strongest.
verified_claims_summary: The independent qpbenchmark v2.3.0 (2024-09-07, i7-6500U laptop, prebuilt wheels through qpsolvers 4.3.3: piqp 0.4.1, osqp 0.6.7.post0) ran 138 Maros-Meszaros problems and ranked PIQP first at every setting. OSQP's shifted geometric mean runtime was 12.7x (default), 16.1x (high accuracy), 52.8x (low) and 51.9x (mid) PIQP's, with failures counted at the 1000 s limit, so the ratios mix speed with OSQP's 21-44% success rate. PIQP's own piqp_benchmarks on a Threadripper 3990X give OSQP 7.55x (low accuracy) and 42.66x (high accuracy).
status_note: Actively maintained (0.6.4 released 2026-08-28, 580 commits, 149 stars, on PyPI and conda-forge) and BSD-2-licensed, so it is safe to adopt; pin 0.6.4 or later for the memory-safety fix.
